title: Can tiles cover a board with two opposite corners removed?
description: An eight by eight board has the top right and bottom left corner squares removed. The board is coloured like a chessboard, and the two removed corners have the same colour. That leaves thirty two of one colour and thirty of the other, but every tile covers one of each.
teaching_notes: One idea: count each colour after the squares are removed, and compare. Watch for students who stop at an even count of squares.

video_script.why: The child uses the chessboard colouring to show that a board with two same coloured corners removed cannot be tiled.
video_script.substitution: Two removed corners of the same colour leave 32 of one colour and 30 of the other, but each tile covers one of each.
video_script.anchor: An 8 × 8 board coloured like a chessboard, with the top right and bottom left corner squares removed, and a tile that covers 2 squares.
video_script.payoff_line: No, the board cannot be tiled, because the two removed corners have the same colour.

final_answer.value: Not possible: the two removed corners have the same colour, leaving 32 of one colour and 30 of the other
final_answer.spoken: not possible, because the two removed corners have the same colour, leaving thirty two of one colour and thirty of the other

hold_back: Not possible: the two removed corners have the same colour, leaving 32 of one colour and 30 of the other
maths_rules: The region has 64 squares minus 2, which is 62 squares, an even number.
Colour it like a chessboard. The top right and bottom left corners have the same colour, say black.
The full board has 32 white and 32 black squares. Removing two black ones leaves 32 white and 30 black.
Each 2 × 1 tile covers one white and one black square.
31 tiles would cover 31 of each colour, but the counts are 32 and 30.
Check: the colour counts are not equal, so no tiling exists.
